chunks: A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — and I was seated (present) — about a pool of water that they came to, and therein was a carcass. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'When the water is overwhelming (in quantity) and the smell is not detected in it, then perform wudu (ablution).'

key_terms.الرِّيح: Smell/odour; one of the three indicators (along with colour and taste) by which change in water quality is judged in fiqh.
key_terms.تَوَضَّأ: Perform wudu (ritual ablution). This is the prerequisite purification act before salat.
key_terms.جِيفَة: A carcass or putrefied corpse of an animal; a source of najasah (ritual impurity).
key_terms.غَدِير: A natural pool or pond of collected water, not a running stream.
key_terms.قَاهِر: Literally 'overpowering, dominant'; in fiqh this refers to water that is abundant enough that impurity cannot alter its properties.

ai.seo_question: Is water containing a dead animal (carcass) permissible for wudu according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted through Abdullah ibn Sinan who was personally present, records a jurisprudential ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) on the permissibility of using water that contains a dead animal. The Imam lays down a practical criterion: if the water is large enough to overwhelm the impurity (i.e., its quantity is dominant) and no foul smell is detectable in it, the water remains ritually pure and may be used for wudu. This establishes the principle that a large body of water can absorb minor contamination without losing its ritual purity.
